newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Gov. proposes $66.6 bln spending plan.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Gov. proposes $66.6 bln spending plan.

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson on Thursday proposed a $66.6 billion state spending plan for fiscal year 1997-1998 that would cut taxes, boost education funding and restructure the state's welfare system.
Wilson, a Republican, told reporters his budget incorporated general fund expenditures of $50.3 billion, below general fund revenues of $50.7 billion, and maintained a reserve of $553 million.
As part of his budget plan, Wilson proposed a 10 percent reduction over the next two years in the state's bank and corporation tax in a bid to improve the business climate.
A $200 million bond was proposed by Wilson to capitalize an Infrastructure Bank to help finance infrastructure projects related to business development.
The budget also proposed the establishment of three new foreign trade offices in Asia and South America.
Wilson's budget proposal would keep primary and secondary education the state's top spending priority at $20.9 billion -- nearly 42 cents of every general fund dollar.
Wilson's school budget included $488 million to fully implement his class size reduction program. It also proposed a $2 billion bond to help implement the plan.

The University of California's total budget was increased by more than $135 million to nearly $3.1 billion, while the California State University system was budgeted to grow by nearly $75 million for a total of nearly $2.5 billion. California's community college budget would increase by nearly $238 million to nearly $4.5 billion.
Wilson said his proposed budgets for higher education would avert the need for student fee increases.
As part of his budget, Wilson unveiled a welfare reform plan replacing the Aid to Families with Dependent Children program with his California Temporary Assistance Plan.
"We need to reform a system that is failing a great many people," Wilson said.

Wilson's welfare plan would establish a state lifetime limit for assistance of five years, and would limit the time a recipient could receive cash benefits to no more than 24 cumulative months in any 36-month period for those already receiving aid. For those applying for aid after January 1, 1998, assistance would be limited to not more than 12-months in any 24-month period.
Under the plan, grants would be reduced by 15 percent for able-bodied recipients after six months on assistance.
Wilson's welfare reform plan also proposed to eliminate the state mandate requiring counties to offer general assistance cash grants to the poor.

Wilson's budget included $1.17 billion in capital outlay, excluding highways and state schools. Funding for this program would come from general obligation bonds, lease revenue bonds, federal funds, general funds and various special funds.

The governor did not propose new general obligation bonds for the state's prison system. Instead, Wilson said the state should use federal prison construction money to build one prison and lease revenue bonds to build two others.

Wilson's budget proposal for 1997-1998 was up $2.4 billion over the current year budget. His new budget assumed the continuation of prior year reductions in health and welfare programs, as well as the elimination of the state's renters tax credit program.
